title: Cap. VIII Resp.: Durandus, Thomas, Gerson — unequal gifts from liberality are not injustice
pass_a_gloss: The Scholastics answer more succinctly, That it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals, where something is given from mere liberality, but where it is rendered from debt. So Durandus book 1, distinction 41, question 2, response to 1. Unto the same sentence Thomas, There is no iniquity with God, if he prepare unequals for equals. For this would be against the reason of justice, if the effect of predestination were rendered from debt, and not given. For from those things which are given from grace, someone can at his pleasure give to whom he will more or less, provided he subtract from none what is owed, Part 1, question 23, article 5, response to 3. Finally Gerson in the Moral Rules affirms the same, There is not acceptance of persons except where there is debt and parity on both sides, because in making gratuitous things to take one, to dismiss another, is not acceptance of persons. From these therefore it is clear that the consequence of the Major in the foresaid argument was plainly null: because in predestination God gives not to the predestined an owed but an unowed grace; and likewise in reprobation he does not deny to the reprobate the benefit of an owed but of an unowed grace.
pass_b_english: The Scholastics answer more briefly: it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals where the gift is from mere liberality — only where something is rendered from debt. So Durandus (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 2 ad 1). Thomas to the same effect: There is no iniquity with God if he prepare unequals for equals. It would be against justice if the effect of predestination were rendered as debt and not given. Of things given from grace, one may at pleasure give more or less to whom he will, provided he subtracts from none what is owed (ST I, q. 23 a. 5 ad 3). Gerson in the Moral Rules: there is no respect of persons except where debt and parity stand on both sides; in free gifts, to take one and dismiss another is not respect of persons. So the major's consequence in the argument is plainly null: in predestination God gives the predestined not owed but unowed grace; in reprobation he denies the reprobate not an owed benefit but an unowed one.
source_text: Scholastici respondent magis succinte, Non esse injustum aut vitiosum dare inaequalia aequalibus, ubi aliquid datur ex mera liberalitate, sed ubi ex debito redditur. Sic Durandus lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. 2. resp. ad 1. In eandem sententiam Thomas, Non est iniquitas apud Deum, si inaequalia aequalibus praeparet. Hoc enim esset contra justitiae rationem, si praedestinationis effectus ex debito redderetur, et non daretur. Ex his enim quae ex gratia dantur, potest aliquis pro libito suo dare cui vult plus vel minus, dummodo nulli subtrahat debitum, Part. 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. resp. ad 3. Denique Gerson in Regulis Moralibus idem affirmat, Non est acceptio personarum nisi ubi debitum est et paritas utrobique, quia in gratis faciendis unum capere, alium dimittere, non est acceptio personarum. Ex hisce igitur perspicuum est, consequentiam Majoris in praedicto argumento fuisse plane nullam: quia in praedestinatione Deus non dat praedestinato debitam sed indebitam gratiam; atque similiter in reprobatione non denegat reprobato debitae sed indebitae gratiae beneficium.
